sections.title: Server power supplies: redundancy, hot-swap, and the density race
ps: Server power supplies live in standardized slots — common form factors let any qualified vendor's unit drop into any compliant server — which turns the competition into a density race: more watts from the same fixed volume, measured in watts per cubic inch

Redundancy comes in flavors: N+1 adds one spare module, while N+N doubles everything, with two independent supply feeds (A and B) each able to carry the full load — the failure of an entire utility path leaves the server unaware

Hot-swap is an engineered trick, not a given: ORing circuits isolate a failed unit so it cannot drag down the shared bus, precharge circuits tame the inrush when a fresh unit slots in live, and firmware rebalances current sharing across the survivors

Redundancy taxes efficiency: two supplies each at half load sit below their efficiency sweet spot, so fleets use techniques like cold redundancy — parking a spare in standby while the active unit runs near its optimum — trading wake-up latency for watts

sections.title: The OCP movement: why hyperscalers publish their hardware
ps: The Open Compute Project inverted hardware secrecy: hyperscalers publish rack, power-shelf, and busbar specifications openly, so any manufacturer can build to them and any operator can adopt them — infrastructure designs as shared standards rather than trade secrets

The publisher's motive is procurement power: an open specification creates multiple interchangeable suppliers competing on execution rather than design lock-in — deliberately commoditizing your own supply base is a buyer's strategy

For suppliers the bargain cuts both ways: a standard socket means lower custom-engineering cost and a bigger addressable market, but rivals fit the same slot — differentiation retreats into efficiency, reliability records, delivery, and price

Open standards also accelerate the industry's clock: a shared baseline lets design improvements propagate fleet-wide in one generation, and the standards process itself — contributions, revisions, certified-compliant products — becomes a place where influence is contested

sections.title: Optoelectronics: light-emitting semiconductors as a business
ps: An LED is a semiconductor junction that emits photons when current crosses it — electroluminescence — converting electricity to light directly instead of heating a filament until it glows, which is why efficacy in lumens per watt rewrote the lighting industry

The same physics runs backward and sideways: photodiodes convert light to current for sensing, infrared LED-sensor pairs handle proximity detection and optical encoding, and optocouplers use a light path to carry signals between circuits that must stay electrically isolated

Commodity opto is a hard business: LEDs and display backlights commoditized brutally, teaching component makers the pattern — differentiate into automotive-grade, sensing, and specialty niches, or watch margins evaporate

The frontier application is data-center interconnect: as clusters scale, copper links run out of reach at high speeds, and the industry moves optical links ever closer to the silicon — making laser and photonics competence a strategic adjacency for electronics groups

sections.title: High-volume manufacturing: the SMT line and the yield religion
ps: A surface-mount technology (SMT) line is electronics' assembly line: solder paste is printed through a stencil, robotic pick-and-place heads set thousands of components per hour, a reflow oven melts everything into place, and automated optical inspection screens the result

Yield is the profit lever: at thin margins, the difference between 98% and 99.5% first-pass yield — fewer boards reworked or scrapped — can represent most of the profitability. Defects are counted per million opportunities and hunted statistically

Power products add a testing burden: in-circuit and functional test, then burn-in — running units hot under load to trigger infant-mortality failures before shipment, because the bathtub curve says early life is when marginal units die

Manufacturing strategy is now geography: concentrating capacity optimizes cost, but customers and tariffs demand diversification, so plants multiply across countries — capacity placement has become part of the sales pitch, not just the cost model

sections.title: Design-win economics: revenue decided years early
ps: A design win means being engineered into a platform: samples submitted years before volume, months of qualification testing, and finally a place on the customer's approved vendor list — after which revenue rides the platform for its production life

Mid-platform switching is rare because requalification is expensive, so competition concentrates at generation boundaries — when a new platform redefines every socket, every seat is briefly winnable, and the qualification race is compressed and decisive

Buyers deliberately keep multiple qualified sources: supply security and price leverage argue for two or three suppliers sharing each socket in negotiated proportions, with share shifting gradually on performance — sole-source positions are rare and precious

Winning increasingly requires betting capital first: buyers award share to suppliers who commit factory capacity ahead of demand, so capex and working capital precede revenue — the balance sheet becomes part of the bid

sections.title: Taiwan's cluster: geography as a competitive weapon
ps: Taiwan concentrates the entire electronics stack — chip foundries, substrates, passives, power components, ODM assembly, and a deep engineering labor pool — within a few hours' drive, so an iteration that takes a week across an ocean happens in a day

The cluster is self-reinforcing: suppliers locate near customers, talent circulates between firms, and shared infrastructure lowers everyone's costs — agglomeration economics, the same force that built every industrial heartland

Its history is a capability ladder: contract assembly in the PC era built manufacturing excellence, which funded design capability, which produced the ODMs that now define server and power hardware — decades of climbing from building things to designing them

Concentration is also the vulnerability: earthquakes, energy dependence, and geopolitics sit under the whole stack at once, so customers now demand geographic diversification — and cluster firms are exporting their model to Southeast Asia, Mexico, and the US, testing whether the magic travels

flashcards.q: What is the difference between N+1 and N+N redundancy?
flashcards.a: N+1 adds one spare module beyond what the load requires — any single failure is covered. N+N doubles the entire system: two independent feeds, each able to carry the full load alone, so even losing an entire utility path is invisible. N+N costs more and runs each side lightly loaded.

flashcards.q: What engineering makes hot-swapping a live power supply safe?
flashcards.a: Three mechanisms: ORing circuits isolate a failed unit so it cannot drag down the shared bus; precharge circuitry tames the inrush when a fresh unit meets charged capacitors; and control firmware rebalances current sharing across the remaining units within microseconds. Without them, removal or insertion would glitch the load.

flashcards.q: Why do hyperscalers publish their rack and power specifications openly?
flashcards.a: Procurement power. An open specification creates multiple interchangeable suppliers competing on execution instead of proprietary lock-in — deliberately commoditizing the supply base. It also standardizes their own global operations and accelerates industry iteration on a shared baseline.

flashcards.q: What does an open standard do to supplier competition?
flashcards.a: It moves differentiation from design to execution: everyone fits the same socket, so suppliers compete on efficiency, reliability records, manufacturing scale, delivery, and price. Custom-engineering costs fall and the addressable market grows — but so does the number of rivals who can credibly bid.

flashcards.q: How does an LED make light, and why did it win?
flashcards.a: Current crossing a semiconductor junction releases energy directly as photons — electroluminescence. An incandescent bulb heats a wire until it glows, wasting most of the energy as heat. Direct conversion multiplied lumens per watt and lifetime, which is why LEDs took over lighting within a generation.

flashcards.q: Why does optical interconnect matter more as AI clusters grow?
flashcards.a: Copper links lose signal rapidly as data rates rise — usable reach shrinks toward a meter or two at modern speeds. Light in fiber carries far more bandwidth much farther, so interconnect moves optical and creeps closer to the silicon — making photonics competence strategic for electronics suppliers.

flashcards.q: What happens on an SMT line?
flashcards.a: Solder paste is stencil-printed onto bare boards, pick-and-place machines set components at thousands per hour, a reflow oven melts the solder to bond everything, and automated optical inspection screens the result. It is electronics' high-speed assembly line — throughput and precision at once.

flashcards.q: Why is first-pass yield the profit lever in high-volume electronics?
flashcards.a: Margins are thin, so the cost of reworking or scrapping defective boards comes straight out of profit. The difference between 98% and 99.5% first-pass yield can represent most of a product line's profitability — which is why defects are counted per million opportunities and attacked statistically.

flashcards.q: What is burn-in testing, and what curve justifies it?
flashcards.a: Running units under load, often at elevated temperature, before shipment to trigger early failures in the factory rather than the field. The bathtub curve justifies it: failure rates run high in early life, flat in midlife, and rise in old age — burn-in consumes the risky first hours in-house.

flashcards.q: What is an approved vendor list, and why does qualification gate everything?
flashcards.a: The AVL is the buyer's roster of suppliers qualified for each component after samples and months of validation. Not on it, no orders — regardless of price. Once on, requalification costs protect your seat, so revenue is decided in the qualification race years before production volume ships.

flashcards.q: Why does supplier competition concentrate at platform generation changes?
flashcards.a: Mid-platform, switching suppliers means expensive requalification, so incumbents keep their sockets. When a new generation redefines every socket, every seat is briefly winnable at once — the qualification race compresses, and positions won then persist for the platform's entire production life.

flashcards.q: What makes an electronics cluster powerful — and fragile?
flashcards.a: Powerful: the whole supply stack and talent pool within hours, so iteration is fast and costs stay low — agglomeration compounds on itself. Fragile: earthquakes, energy dependence, and geopolitics sit beneath everything at once, driving customers to demand the geographic diversification cluster firms must now deliver abroad.
